Incremental authorizations by definition happen after the original authorization has completed, so keeping the CVC for them means storing SAD after authorization. This is the case the cited requirements are generally understood to prohibit; the clause wording still needs confirming against the standard.

If confirmed, rewrite 12.4 and NFR-6 so the CVC is purged when the first authorization reaches a final outcome (or when the cascade ends). Remove CVC from incremental authorizations and use scheme stored-credential/incremental indicators instead. Update the 'CVC handling' confirmed decision and the NFR-6 test so it asserts the CVC is absent after authorization completes.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Keeps the NFR-5 Level 1 assessment achievable and avoids building a non-compliant Vault.
recommendation.issue: The CVC retention policy rests on a reading of PCI DSS v4.0 Req. 3.2.1/3.3.2 that has not been checked and is probably wrong.
recommendation.rationale: If SAD may not be kept after authorization, the Vault design, NFR-6 and the cascade and incremental-auth flows all fail the QSA assessment.
recommendation.verification: Written QSA opinion on file. The NFR-6 test asserts no CVC exists in the Vault after the final authorization outcome.

findings.statement: Section 12.4 stores the CVC encrypted until settlement or for up to 72 hours. It also re-uses it for cascades and for incremental authorizations, which happen after the first authorization. The design says PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept until settlement. The usual reading of the standard is that SAD may not be kept after authorization completes, and the requirements cited appear to cover storage before authorization, not after. If that reading is right, NFR-6 itself rests on a wrong premise, NFR-5 (Level 1 Report on Compliance) cannot be achieved, and the incremental-authorization use case is unlawful under the standard as built. No external source was available here to confirm the clause wording, so it must be checked before the Vault is built.
findings.title: CVC retained after authorization, citing a PCI DSS allowance that appears not to exist

900 TPS with a ~5 KB completion write (about 5 WCU) plus a lock write, plus LSI write amplification, comes to roughly 5,000-10,000 WCU/s on one partition-key value. If the per-partition limit is 1,000 WCU/s and LSI tables cannot split item collections, that exceeds it several times over.

next_step.action: Confirm the DynamoDB limits and run a hot-key load test before Phase 3.

recommendation.change_summary: Check the per-partition WCU limit and the LSI item-collection constraints against current AWS documentation. Redesign the 9.2/9.3 key as PK = merchant_id#idempotency_key with no LSI. Serve the 'recent requests by merchant' view from a GSI with a sharded key or from Aurora. Store large response bodies by reference. Recompute WCU per write.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-1 and NFR-2 can be met for the largest merchant during campaign events.
recommendation.issue: The idempotency table's capacity claim rests on an unverified, probably overstated, per-partition limit and an under-counted WCU estimate.
recommendation.rationale: Throttling on the hot merchant's partition would reject or delay create-payment calls at peak.
recommendation.verification: Load test: a single merchant at 900 TPS (with 1,350 TPS headroom) against the table shows zero ThrottledRequests.

findings.statement: Section 9.3 says one partition sustains 10,000 WCU/s and that M-0001 needs about 1,800 WCU at peak. DynamoDB's documented per-partition write limit is generally understood to be 1,000 WCU/s. The estimate also ignores two things: completion items carry up to a 4 KB response body, so several WCU per write, and the LSI adds write cost. Tables with an LSI also cannot split an item collection, which caps each partition-key value (here, each merchant). If those limits apply, the largest merchant's idempotency writes will be throttled at campaign peak, failing NFR-1/NFR-2 for 45% of traffic. The confirmed key schema (PK merchant_id plus LSI) is the cause.
findings.title: DynamoDB per-partition write ceiling and WCU arithmetic look wrong for the hot merchant partition

Order identifiers such as '10001' are very likely to repeat across 15,000 merchants within 24 hours. A merchant-agnostic cache key with no hash check would then serve one merchant another merchant's response.

findings.statement: The fast-path cache key is idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, without the merchant. A cache hit returns the stored response with no body-hash check. The document also says merchants often use their own order or invoice numbers as keys. Two merchants with the same key would receive each other's payment responses (a cross-tenant data leak), and a reused key with a different body would not get the 422 required by FR-5. This breaks P3.
findings.title: Redis fast path assumes idempotency keys are globally unique, but they are scoped per merchant

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings even if a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 relies on storage-level asynchronous replication with typical lag under one second, so commits in the last second(s) before a regional loss can be lost. The NFR-4 test (every posting committed before the failure is present after failover) would then fail. The idempotency and outbox state in DynamoDB and MSK, which are not replicated, adds further exposure: an acquirer may have authorized a payment whose record never reached Jakarta.
findings.title: Zero RPO on region loss is claimed over asynchronous Aurora Global Database replication

findings.statement: Every detokenise unwraps a DEK in the HSM (no caching), yet the cluster has one HSM in one AZ. Recovery means creating a new HSM from backup, with no stated restore time. Card peak is about 55% of 2,000 = 1,100 TPS, so the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM is never reached at design load. Meanwhile cascades and the Fraud Hook add detokenise calls on top of that load. Losing the HSM or its AZ stops all card payments, which threatens NFR-3 (99.95%) and the AZ-resilience claims in 20.1. The 20 ms 'vendor benchmark' figure also has not been checked against single-HSM throughput at this load.
findings.title: Single-HSM topology, and a 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM that design volumes never reach
